clinicalPearls: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) targets HuD and related RNA-binding proteins expressed in neuronal nuclei; the antibody is a serum and cerebrospinal fluid marker while cytotoxic T cells are the principal effectors of neuronal injury.
Strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma; in children the same reactivity accompanies neuroblastoma.

Presentation is typically multifocal, with subacute sensory neuronopathy, limbic and brainstem encephalitis, cerebellar involvement and autonomic failure coexisting as paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis.
The sensory neuronopathy (dorsal root ganglionopathy) is often asymmetric, affects all sensory modalities including proprioception, and can produce disabling sensory ataxia and pseudoathetosis.
Autonomic involvement may dominate, with gastrointestinal dysmotility and chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, orthostatic hypotension and pupillary abnormalities.
The neurological syndrome usually precedes the cancer diagnosis, so a positive antibody mandates an intensive tumour search even when initial imaging is unremarkable.
Because the antigen is intracellular, response to immunotherapy is generally poor; prompt treatment of the underlying tumour offers the best chance of neurological stabilisation.
High antibody titres in an appropriate clinical context are highly specific, but low titres can occasionally be seen in a patient with malignancy but without overt neurological disease.
reference.pathophysiology: The Hu antigens (HuD, HuC and Hel-N1) are neuron-restricted RNA-binding proteins that regulate messenger RNA stability and neuronal differentiation. When a tumour, most often small cell lung carcinoma or childhood neuroblastoma, ectopically expresses these proteins, immune tolerance is broken and an onconeural immune response is generated. Although anti-Hu antibody is a reliable diagnostic marker, the antigen is intracellular and inaccessible to circulating antibody, so tissue damage is driven principally by antigen-specific cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes together with activated microglia. This T-cell attack produces inflammatory infiltrates and irreversible neuronal loss across widely distributed populations, including dorsal root ganglia (sensory neuronopathy), the limbic system and brainstem (encephalomyelitis), the cerebellum, and the enteric myenteric plexus (dysautonomia and pseudo-obstruction), explaining the characteristically multifocal clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Other onconeural antibody syndromes such as anti-CV2/CRMP5 or anti-amphiphysin, which may coexist
Vitamin B6 toxicity or vitamin E deficiency causing sensory ataxia
Autoimmune limbic encephalitis from surface-antigen antibodies such as anti-LGI1 or anti-NMDA receptor
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-Hu (ANNA-1) testing with confirmatory immunohistochemistry and line blot
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and whole-body FDG-PET to detect small cell lung carcinoma
Nerve conduction studies showing reduced or absent sensory action potentials with relatively preserved motor responses
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
MRI of the brain to assess medial temporal and brainstem signal change
Autonomic function testing and gastrointestinal transit studies where dysautonomia is suspected
In children, urinary catecholamine metabolites and MIBG imaging to evaluate for neuroblastoma
redFlags: Rapidly progressive sensory ataxia with autonomic failure signalling active encephalomyelitis
Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction with risk of malnutrition and bowel perforation
New or occult small cell lung carcinoma requiring urgent staging
Brainstem involvement threatening bulbar and respiratory function
reference.prognosis: The neurological outcome is generally poor because T-cell-mediated neuronal loss is largely irreversible, and early tumour treatment offers the best chance of halting progression rather than reversing deficits. Overall survival is determined by the combined burden of neurological disability and the underlying malignancy.
pitfalls: Attributing sensory symptoms to chemotherapy toxicity and missing the paraneoplastic cause
Abandoning the tumour search after a single negative CT, when repeated imaging and FDG-PET over time may be required
Expecting immunotherapy alone to reverse deficits without addressing the malignancy
Overlooking coexisting onconeural antibodies that broaden the tumour association
Misreading early autonomic gastrointestinal symptoms as a primary motility disorder
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Do not wait for antibody confirmation to start treatment when clinical suspicion is high; exclude viral and bacterial infection first, then treat.
Test both serum and CSF for anti-Hu (ANNA-1), since sensitivity and specificity differ between the two.

Pursue an intensive tumour search focused on the chest for small cell lung carcinoma, the dominant association; repeat an initially negative malignancy screen every four to six months for up to two years.

Treat the underlying small cell lung carcinoma promptly using standard oncologic staging and treatment-intent pathways; this is the intervention most likely to halt neurological progression, though it is less reliable at reversing deficits than in ectopic-hormone paraneoplastic syndromes.

Start acute immunotherapy without waiting for antibody results once infection is excluded; first line is corticosteroid therapy (intravenous methylprednisolone or oral prednisone-class agents), with intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange as alternative or add-on first-line options.
Set realistic expectations: because the T-cell-mediated neuronal injury is largely irreversible, immunotherapy aims for stabilisation rather than reversal of established deficits.
For non-responders to first-line therapy, consider second-line steroid-sparing/immunosuppressive agents such as rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide.
Tocilizumab (an interleukin-6-directed antibody) may be considered for rituximab-refractory disease, per general autoimmune-encephalitis practice rather than this disease's specific reference source.
Provide symptomatic pain treatment and rehabilitation for neuropathic pain and sensory ataxia from sensory neuronopathy.

Provide supportive and prokinetic management for autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction), with proactive monitoring given the risk of malnutrition and bowel perforation.
Use antiseizure medication for encephalitic seizures and supportive neuropsychiatric care for behavioural or cognitive symptoms.
Escalate monitoring and care intensity for red flags: bulbar or respiratory threat from brainstem involvement, and dysautonomia with arrhythmia risk.

Track disease course with serial clinical neurological assessment and continued surveillance imaging on the repeat-screening schedule; antibody titre is not a validated marker of treatment response and should not replace clinical and tumour-directed follow-up.

Refer early to neurology for diagnostic confirmation and immunotherapy selection, to oncology/pulmonology for tumour staging and treatment, and to rehabilitation and gastroenterology as needed, with ongoing multidisciplinary (including palliative care) follow-up.
